title: Problem Details for HTTP APIs
summary: This standards-track RFC defines a problem detail as a machine-readable way to carry error details in an HTTP response, so that HTTP APIs do not each need to invent their own error format. It was replaced by RFC 9457.

plainLanguage.summary: When a web service has a problem, it can reply in a standard shape that programs understand, instead of every service inventing its own sort of error note.

subtitle: A standard JSON or XML shape for telling API clients exactly what went wrong.

tldr.problem: HTTP status codes are often not enough to tell a program why a request failed, and every HTTP API ended up inventing its own error format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a problem details object with members such as type, title, status, detail and instance, carried as application/problem+json or application/problem+xml.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7807 was replaced by RFC 9457, which is the current definition.

today: RFC 7807 has been obsoleted by RFC 9457, which is now the definition of problem details for HTTP APIs.

sections.title: Why Status Codes Are Not Enough
sections.content:
HTTP status codes sometimes do not carry enough information to be helpful. A person using a browser can read an HTML error page, but programs that consume HTTP APIs usually cannot.

The RFC gives an example: an account without enough credit. A 403 Forbidden tells generic software such as client libraries, caches and proxies the general meaning of the response. It does not say why the request was forbidden, what the balance is, or how to fix it. Putting those details in the body in a machine-readable format lets the client react, for example by topping up the account.

The aim is a common error format for applications that need one, so they are not tempted to redefine the meaning of existing status codes.
sections.plainLanguage: A red stop sign says you cannot go, but not why. Problem details add a little note under the sign explaining the reason, in a way a robot can read.

sections.title: The Problem Details Object
sections.content:
The canonical model is a JSON object. When sent as JSON it uses the application/problem+json media type. A problem details object can have five members:

  • type: a URI reference that identifies the problem type. If absent, it is assumed to be about:blank.
  • title: a short, human-readable summary of the problem type. It SHOULD NOT change between occurrences, except for localization.
  • status: the HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence.
  • detail: a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence.
  • instance: a URI reference that identifies this specific occurrence of the problem.

Consumers MUST use the type string as the primary identifier of the problem type, and SHOULD NOT automatically dereference it. The detail member should help the client correct the problem, and consumers SHOULD NOT parse it for information.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a form with a few boxes: what kind of problem, a short name, the number code, the story of this one time, and a label for this exact event.

sections.title: Extension Members
sections.content:
A problem type definition MAY add more members to the object. In the RFC's example, an out-of-credit problem adds balance and accounts. Another example carries an invalid-params list so that several sub-problems can be reported in one response, provided they are similar enough to share one status code. If they are not, the RFC says the 207 (Multi-Status) code could be used.

Clients MUST ignore extensions they do not recognize, so problem types can grow over time. Because extensions live in a namespace set by the problem type, defining a new standard member would require a new media type.

Names of added members SHOULD start with a letter, use only letters, digits and underscore, and be three characters or longer, so they can be serialized in formats other than JSON.
sections.plainLanguage: A problem note can have extra pockets for special information. If you find a pocket you do not understand, you just leave it alone.

sections.title: Defining New Problem Types
sections.content:
Problem details are not a debugging tool for the implementation. They expose detail about the HTTP interface itself. Truly generic conditions are usually better as plain status codes: a 403 Forbidden in response to a PUT already explains a disallowed write. Problem details are also not meant to replace error formats an application already has.

A new problem type definition MUST document a type URI (typically using http or https), a short title, and the HTTP status code it is used with. It MAY specify use of the Retry-After header. The type URI SHOULD resolve to HTML documentation that explains how to resolve the problem.

The RFC reserves one URI: about:blank means the problem has no semantics beyond the HTTP status code. Its title SHOULD then match the standard status phrase, such as Not Found for 404.
sections.plainLanguage: Before inventing a new kind of problem note, check you really need one. Each new kind needs a name, a short label and the number code it goes with.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The information placed in a problem must be carefully vetted, both when a type is defined and when a problem is generated. Risks include leaking details that could be used to compromise the system, access to it, or users' privacy. Generators are encouraged not to expose implementation details such as a stack dump.

The status member duplicates the HTTP status code, so the two can disagree, for example if a proxy or cache changed the code in transit. The RFC notes that generic software such as proxies, load balancers, firewalls and virus scanners is unlikely to know about the status carried in this member. Generators MUST use the same code in the actual HTTP response.
sections.plainLanguage: When you explain a problem, do not accidentally tell secrets about how the machine works inside. Keep the note helpful but safe.

sections.title: Media Types and the XML Form
sections.content: The RFC registers two media types: application/problem+json and application/problem+xml. Both list HTTP as the application that uses them, take no required parameters, and name the IESG as change controller. Appendix A defines the equivalent XML format.
sections.plainLanguage: The note can be written in two languages, JSON or XML, and each gets its own official name tag so programs know which one they hold.

data.title: Out-of-credit problem
data.code:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Content-Language: en

{
 "type": "https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit",
 "title": "You do not have enough credit.",
 "detail": "Your current balance is 30, but that costs 50.",
 "instance": "/account/12345/msgs/abc",
 "balance": 30,
 "accounts": ["/account/12345",
              "/account/67890"]
}
